newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's Maharaj against full port privatisation.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's Maharaj against full port privatisation.

text.p: Transport Minister Mac Maharaj slammed the door on the total privatisation of South Africa's seven commercial harbours on Wednesday, but left the door open to the partial privatisation of some port operations.

Maharaj said in an opening address to the National Maritime Conference in Cape Town that the land, seawalls, breakwaters and quays of South Africa's ports would always remain the property of the state.
"Whether the operation of the ports should be the responsibility of the state is contentious. The issues are complex...," he said.
Maharaj said partial privatisation of some port operations might be possible.
"Port operations cannot be allowed to become private monopolies. The merits of privatisation must be weighed against the interests of the public.
"At this stage in the debate, I believe the controversial issues should be left to the government to resolve and I can assure you that wisdom will prevail," he said.
In papers prepared for presentation at the conference, delegates who addressed the issue unanimously supported a private-sector role in port operations.
"Efficiency in the operation of cargo terminals can be achieved only through the rigor of private enterprise," said Bernal Floor of Transport Research Associates.
"The pursuit of economic efficiency which has led to deregulation and privatisation in the transportation industries must extend to ports."
South Africa has made the full or partial privatisation of some state assets a central pillar of its macroeconomic strategy for growth, employment and redistribution, known as GEAR.
The state-owned Telkom telecommunications corporation recently announced the sale of a 30 percent stake to a consortium of Malaysian and U.S. operators for $1.26 billion.
Maharaj is expected on Thursday to shortlist buyers seeking to take over the internal Sunair airline and talks are underway about the sale of stakes in other state transport enterprises.
Rennies Group executive director Derek Lawrance said South Africa's ports clearly needed the managerial and commerical skills of the private sector to remain competitive.
"That these skills are needed is clear. Whether they will be accepted, or accepted in one form or another, remains to be seen," he said.

Felix Scheder-Bieschin of Macs Maritime Carriers warned that failure to introduce private enterprise to South Africa's ports would encourage shippers to look elsewhere and could promote the development of Maputo as a Mozambican rival.
"We must realise that the national patronage and monopoly omnipresent in these ports have outlived themselves and now stand in the way of private entrepreneurship," he said.
Maharaj did not stay on after his opening address, but said he had delegated officials to follow the conference and brief him on its major themes.
